meta.title: A Platform Modernization Story
meta.voiceDirection: Wes Anderson register: a chronicler reading from a ledger. Deadpan, unhurried, faintly amused, never excited. Numbers read evenly, like an inventory.
meta.pauseNote: No SSML. Pauses come from line breaks - each sentence sits on its own line, blank-line separated. Keep the blank lines when pasting.

scenes.text:
A platform modernization.

In four acts.

Faster.

Lighter.

Built to scale.

Those were the instructions.

What follows is what happened.

Act One.

The Weight of Growth.

Every success arrived carrying luggage.

Thirteen megabytes, on every visit.

Six seconds before anything appeared.

And fifteen filter systems — each of them slightly different.

Act Two.

The Rebuild.

They began, as one does, by deleting things.

Two hundred twenty-nine commits.

One thousand seven hundred sixty-eight files.

They deleted more than they wrote.

On purpose.

The application had been shipped as one enormous parcel.

It was opened, sorted, and repacked.

Two hundred forty-nine smaller ones.

This is where the weight had been living.

Four bundles, comfortable, undisturbed, and downloaded by every single visitor.

Previously, the dashboard asked for everything.

Now it asks for what the dashboard needs.

A modest idea, arrived at late.

Without preload, the browser discovers its files one after another.

With it, it collects the important ones at once.

The page begins sooner.

Consider the sidebar.

The pointer merely rests on Inbox — it does not click — and the page's bundles begin arriving quietly in the background.

Assets only.

Zero requests to the server.

Nobody has decided anything yet.

One function.

Three hundred fifty-seven kilobytes.

Delivered faithfully, on every page load, to people who never once used it.

The remedy was a single line.

Three hundred fifty-seven kilobytes became zero.

These are the most satisfying repairs, and the least visible.

Time to paint: halved.

The screen now arrives before the user has finished deciding to wait for it.

For years the build required twelve gigabytes of heap and a ten-gigabyte swap file, to keep it from collapsing.

Rolldown bundles in Rust — off the Node heap entirely.

So the swap file was deleted.

The heap fell to four.

The scaffolding came down, because the building no longer falls down.
Certain lessons were written down, so that they would not have to be learned a second time.

The styles had been living inside the JavaScript, recomputed in the browser on every render.

They were moved into ordinary files.

They are now computed once — by the build.

Cascade layers decide who wins.

Ours are ordered; the last one always does.

Then version six arrived with unlayered styles — outside every layer, and therefore above them all.

This was handled.

There had been fifteen filter systems.

One fix required fifteen fixes.

They became a single configuration-driven module — roughly sixty-five percent of the filter layer, simply gone.

One filter now.

The same pills, the same saved views, across fifteen pages that had never once agreed.

It can be operated entirely by keyboard.

The people who work here all day tend to notice this first.

Architecture that compounds.

Each thing built on it is cheaper than the thing before it.

Formerly, every tile fetched at once, whether or not you looked at it.

Now a tile fetches when it enters view.

Not before.

The list renders only what is on screen.

A thousand rows, or ten.

The browser cannot tell the difference.

Your place is kept in the address bar.

The filters, the page, the customer — all of it.

You may now send a colleague a link and be entirely confident about what they will see.

React eighteen.

Vite eight.

React Query.

The foundation was replaced while the building remained open.

Four leaks were found in the startup path.

Objects created on every render, and never once closed.

They are closed now.

Act Three.

The Payoff.

What all of it actually bought.

The dashboard loads in seven hundred fifty-five milliseconds.

Two and a half megabytes.

Fourteen startup calls, where there had been forty-three.

Every line moves in the same direction.

This is rarer than it sounds, and was not guaranteed.

Two thirds less code was written.

Compression did the remaining third.

We cite the bytes that crossed the network — those are the ones the user waits for.

The build once took one minute and forty-four seconds.

It now takes fifteen.

Ninety seconds returned, on every push, to every engineer, forever.

Some honesty, briefly.

Different deployments.

Different datasets.

Cold loads.

Read the direction — and not the decimals.

One filter system.

Not fifteen.

If you remember a single line, we would prefer it were that one.

It loads two and a half times faster.

The feeds no longer freeze.

Customers did not need to be told any of this.

One toolkit.

Less code to own.

The team now spends its time on things that did not exist last year.

Act Four.

The Agents.

A fast build introduced a new kind of mistake.

The component library now ships its own expertise.

Alfred keeps the house.

He does not write code.

He determines who should.

A quick question, you look up yourself.

A real job is sent away — and reports back.

Neo reads every pull request before anyone else does.

On this one, it found a command-injection hole — in the workflow written to harden the pipeline.

One dollar and seventy-six cents.

Seven and a half minutes.

No human had opened the file.

The platform, re-engineered.

Faster, lighter, and considerably harder to break.

Thank you for your attention.
